issues.legal_issue: A stipulated sum payable upon breach of an agreement to transfer immovable property does not, by itself, rebut the presumption that monetary compensation is inadequate when the agreement does not make payment an alternative to performance.
material_facts: The agreement to sell the property required the seller, in the event of breach, to refund the advance and pay an additional stipulated sum as damages.
The agreement did not give the seller an option to pay the stipulated sum instead of completing the sale.
The courts found that the seller had not established fraud, misrepresentation, or an unfair advantage obtained by the buyer.
issues.conclusion: The stipulated damages clause was only evidence bearing on whether the presumption was rebutted; it was not conclusive, and the presumption was not rebutted in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, the court presumes that breach of a contract to transfer immovable property cannot be adequately relieved by monetary compensation unless the contrary is proved. Section 20 permits specific performance despite a sum named for breach, unless the contract makes payment an alternative to performance; section 22 makes specific relief discretionary on sound judicial grounds. The corresponding provisions are sections 10, 23, and 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The court also relied on the distinction described in Sir Edward Fry’s treatise between a sum securing performance and payment as an elected alternative to performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and immovable_property_transfer and breach_sum_stipulated and no_payment_option

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant sought specific performance of an agreement to transfer immovable property.
predicates.immovable_property_transfer: The agreement required one party to transfer immovable property to another.
predicates.breach_sum_stipulated: The agreement named a sum payable in the event of breach.
predicates.no_payment_option: The agreement did not allow the party in default to choose payment of the stipulated sum instead of performance.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks specific performance of an agreement to transfer immovable property, a stipulated breach sum without an option to pay instead of performing does not, by itself, rebut the presumption that money is inadequate.

issues.legal_issue: Rebutting the presumption that monetary compensation is inadequate does not automatically establish that compensation is adequate or bar specific performance.
material_facts: The defendants argued that removal of the statutory presumption would automatically make the bar to specific performance apply.
The court held that the bar depends on proof that monetary compensation is adequate on the facts of the particular case.
The evidence did not establish the extent of prospective gains lost through the property’s depreciation, or provide a standard for assessing that loss.
The presumption was not rebutted on the evidence in this case.
issues.conclusion: The bar to specific performance applies only when monetary compensation is actually proved adequate; rebutting the presumption alone does not trigger the bar.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, read together, require actual proof that monetary compensation is adequate before the bar to specific performance operates. The corresponding provisions are sections 10 and 14 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Once the presumption is rebutted, the claimant may still prove by other evidence that money would not adequately compensate for the breach.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and immovable_property_transfer and inadequacy_presumption_rebutted and monetary_adequacy_proven

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant sought specific performance of an agreement to transfer immovable property.
predicates.immovable_property_transfer: The agreement required one party to transfer immovable property to another.
predicates.inadequacy_presumption_rebutted: Evidence established the contrary of the presumption that monetary compensation would be inadequate.
predicates.monetary_adequacy_proven: Evidence established that monetary compensation would adequately remedy the breach in the circumstances of the case.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit involving immovable property, rebutting the presumption of monetary inadequacy leads to a bar only when evidence also proves that monetary compensation is adequate.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may correct a trial court’s exercise of discretion to deny specific performance when that exercise rests on an unsound or unsupported ground.
material_facts: The trial court denied specific performance because it considered that the buyer had obtained an unfair advantage.
The appellate court found that the buyer had not obtained an unfair advantage and that the seller had been in the stronger bargaining position.
The trial court’s basis for exercising its discretion was found to be untenable and unsound.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court rightly corrected the trial court’s exercise of discretion and decreed specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, provides that discretion to grant specific relief must be exercised on sound and reasonable grounds, guided by judicial principles and capable of correction on appeal. The corresponding provision is section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

predicates.appeal_from_specific_performance_discret: The proceeding was an appeal concerning a trial court’s discretionary decision on specific performance.
predicates.trial_court_denied_specific_performance: The trial court refused to order specific performance.
predicates.denial_rest_on_unsound_ground: The refusal rested on a ground that was unsupported or unsound in light of the facts.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a trial court’s refusal of specific performance and that refusal rests on an unsupported or unsound ground, the appellate court may properly correct the exercise of discretion.
